lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Shopping and Bargaining in Chinese â An African Buyer's Toolkit

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in the Shopping and Bargaining module into a single working document for African entrepreneurs, traders, and procurement officers who source clothing, textiles, and souvenirs in Chinese-speaking markets. Whether you are buying wholesale garments in Guangzhou, negotiating fabric in Yiwu, or picking up gifts in Nairobi's Chinatown, the language and etiquette you use directly affects your margin. This reference gives you the vocabulary, the numbers, the payment routes, and the negotiation scripts â plus the cultural guardrails â to close deals confidently and profitably.

1. Clothing and Colours: The Vocabulary You Will Actually Use

Colour and garment vocabulary is the foundation of any clothing transaction. In Chinese wholesale markets, sellers will often quote a price per piece and then ask which colour and size you want. If you cannot name the colour quickly, you lose momentum and the seller may assume you are a tourist rather than a buyer. Learn the core colour terms and the garment nouns before you enter the market.

Table 1: Core clothing and colour vocabulary for Chinese market buying

Source: Vocabulary compiled from HSK 1â3 standard word lists (Hanban/Chinese Testing International) and common market usage documented in ChinesePod and Hacking Chinese learner resources.

2. Sizes, Trying On, and Fitting Rooms

Chinese sizing runs smaller than European, American, and many African standard sizes. A Chinese "L" (å¤§å·) often corresponds to a European "M" or even "S". Always ask to try the item on (å¯ä»¥è¯ç©¿å? â kÄyÇ shÃ¬chuÄn ma?) and confirm the fitting room location (è¯è¡£é´ â shÃ¬yÄ«jiÄn). In wholesale markets, fitting rooms may be shared or non-existent; in that case, ask the seller to hold the item against you or measure it flat. For bulk orders, request a size chart (å°ºç è¡¨ â chÇmÇ biÇo) in writing so you can compare against your home market measurements before shipping.

Table 2: Indicative size conversion and payment methods for African buyers in Chinese markets

Source: Size conversion adapted from China Briefing sourcing guidance and HKTDC apparel export documentation. African fit notes based on common West and East African retail sizing patterns.

3. Asking for Prices and Discounts

The core question is å¤å°é±? (duÅshÇo qiÃ¡n?) â "How much?" For bulk pricing, ask æ¹åä»·æ¯å¤å°? (pÄ«fÄ jiÃ  shÃ¬ duÅshÇo?) â "What is the wholesale price?" When the quote is too high, respond with å¤ªè´µäº (tÃ i guÃ¬ le) â "Too expensive" â and follow with ä¾¿å®ä¸ç¹ (piÃ¡nyi yÄ«diÇn) â "A little cheaper." A stronger lever is volume: æä¹°å¾å¤ (wÇ mÇi hÄn duÅ) â "I am buying a lot" â or å¤ä¹°å ä»¶å¯ä»¥ä¾¿å®å? (duÅ mÇi jÇ jiÃ n kÄyÇ piÃ¡nyi ma?) â "If I buy several pieces, can it be cheaper?"

4. Bargaining Phrases and Etiquette

Bargaining in Chinese markets is expected, but it is a social ritual, not a confrontation. Keep it friendly, smile, and never insult the goods. Useful phrases include åä¾¿å®ä¸ç¹å§ (zÃ i piÃ¡nyi yÄ«diÇn ba) â "Make it a bit cheaper" â and åè®©ä¸æ­¥ (gÃ¨ rÃ ng yÄ« bÃ¹) â "Let's each give a little." If the price is still wrong, thank the seller and walk away slowly; a genuine seller will often call you back with a better offer. In wholesale markets, the price is often already close to the floor, so aggressive bargaining can damage a long-term supplier relationship. For repeat business, prioritise reliability and quality over squeezing the last few yuan.

â ï¸ Safety Warning â Cash, Cards, and Mobile Payment

Never carry large amounts of cash in open markets. In China, mobile payment (WeChat Pay å¾®ä¿¡æ¯ä» and Alipay æ¯ä»å®) is dominant; foreign cards are often not accepted. If you are a foreign buyer, set up WeChat Pay or Alipay with an international card before you travel, or use a licensed currency exchange. Avoid informal "money changers" on the street â they are a common source of counterfeit notes and theft. In African markets with Chinese traders, confirm the accepted payment method before agreeing a price, and always ask for a receipt (æ¶æ® â shÅujÃ¹) for business records and customs clearance.

5. Paying: Cash, Card, and Mobile Payment

Payment method affects your bargaining power. Cash (ç°é â xiÃ njÄ«n) is still accepted in many markets and can sometimes secure a small discount, but it carries risk. Bank cards (é¶è¡å¡ â yÃ­nhÃ¡ngkÇ) are accepted in larger stores and malls, but not in most wholesale stalls. Mobile payment via WeChat Pay (å¾®ä¿¡æ¯ä» â WÄixÃ¬n zhÄ«fÃ¹) and Alipay (æ¯ä»å® â ZhÄ«fÃ¹bÇo) is the standard in China; as of 2024, both platforms support international cards for foreign visitors, but you must set this up before you arrive. In African markets, mobile money (M-Pesa, MTN MoMo, Airtel Money) is often the fastest route, but Chinese wholesalers may prefer cash or WeChat. Always confirm the exchange rate and any transaction fees before paying.

6. Role-Play: Buying a Souvenir â A Worked Script

You: ä½ å¥½ï¼è¿ä¸ªå¤å°é±? (NÇ hÇo, zhÃ¨ge duÅshÇo qiÃ¡n?) â Hello, how much is this?
Seller: ä¸¤ç¾åã (LiÇng bÇi kuÃ i.) â 200 yuan.
You: å¤ªè´µäºï¼ä¾¿å®ä¸ç¹å§ã (TÃ i guÃ¬ le, piÃ¡nyi yÄ«diÇn ba.) â Too expensive, make it cheaper.
Seller: ä¸ç¾å«ã (YÄ« bÇi bÄ.) â 180.
You: æä¹°ä¸ä¸ªï¼ä¸å±åç¾äºï¼å¯ä»¥å? (WÇ mÇi sÄn gÃ¨, yÄ«gÃ²ng sÃ¬ bÇi wÇ, kÄyÇ ma?) â I'll buy three, 450 total, okay?
Seller: å¥½å§ï¼æäº¤! (HÇo ba, chÃ©ngjiÄo!) â Okay, deal!

This script works because it bundles volume with a round-number offer, which is easier for the seller to accept than a small incremental discount. For business buyers, always ask for a receipt and, where possible, a business card (åç â mÃ­ngpiÃ n) so you can follow up for repeat orders.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Learn colour and garment vocabulary before entering the market â it signals you are a serious buyer.
  • Check Chinese sizing against your home market measurements; request a written size chart for bulk orders.
  • Always ask å¤å°é±? and, for volume, æ¹åä»·æ¯å¤å°?
  • Use å¤ªè´µäº and ä¾¿å®ä¸ç¹ politely â never insult the goods or the seller.
  • Bundle multiple items into one round-number offer to close faster.
  • Confirm payment method before agreeing a price; set up WeChat Pay or Alipay in advance if buying in China.
  • Always request a receipt (æ¶æ®) for business records and customs clearance.
  • Walk away slowly if the price is wrong â a genuine seller will often call you back.

Further Reading

  • ChinesePod â Shopping and Bargaining lesson series (free trial lessons available).
  • Hacking Chinese â Practical vocabulary and market survival guides.
  • China Briefing â Sourcing and supplier guides for international buyers.
  • HKTDC â Apparel export and sizing documentation.
  • Visa â Guide to using international cards with WeChat Pay and Alipay in China.

Business takeaway: In Chinese-speaking markets, language is leverage. The buyer who can name the colour, confirm the size, ask for the wholesale price, and pay through the right channel closes better deals and builds supplier relationships that survive beyond a single transaction. For African traders, this is not just vocabulary â it is margin.
